Q: How do I move my git project to a subdirectory for all commits, except one file? A:

git-filter-repo has an --invert-paths option that does exactly what OP is asking for.

https://github.com/newren/git-filter-repo/blob/c1d8461ee34c6d3f987e0f19191f2105cb2a33c8/Documentation/git-filter-repo.txt#L106-L109

--invert-paths::
    Invert the selection of files from the specified
    --path-{match,glob,regex} options below, i.e. only select
    files matching none of those options.

So, using that that option, you run:

 git filter-repo --path .gitattributes --invert-paths --to-subdirectory-filter ProjectA/

Q: How does ending a subobject lifetime impact enclosing object and other subobjects? A:

For ease of naming, I'm going to modify your code slightly:

alignas(A) std::byte Storage[sizeof(A)];
auto* pA = std::construct_at(reinterpret_cast<A*>(Storage), 1., 2, 3., 4., 5.);
// There is a live A object in Storage
auto* pNotC1 = std::construct_at(
    reinterpret_cast<std::uint16_t*>(Storage + offsetof(A, c1)),
    std::uint16_t{0});

by adding two pointers. These pointers don't change anything about the answer, they just let me name stuff easier. I also named it Storage with a capital letter, to not confuse it with the standard term.

[basic.life]/2.2-2.5:

The lifetime of an object o of type T ends when:

[...]

the storage which the object occupies is released, or is reused by an object that is not nested within o

[intro.object]/4:

4 An object a is nested within another object b if
(4.1) a is a subobject of b, or
(4.2) b provides storage for a, or
(4.3) there exists an object c where a is nested within c, and c is nested within b.

[intro.object]/3:

If a complete object is created ([expr.new]) in storage associated with another object e of type “array of N unsigned char” or of type “array of N std​::​byte” ([cstddef.syn]), that array provides storage for the created object if
(3.1) the lifetime of e has begun and not ended, and
(3.2) the storage for the new object fits entirely within e, and
(3.3) there is no array object that satisfies these constraints nested within e.

At the point right after we construct *pA:

The Storage array provides-storage for the *pA object. The *pA object is nested-within Storage.

pA->c1 is also nested-within *pA, and as such is nested-within Storage.

We then construct *pNotC1. The lifetime of *pA and Storage are at stake here, as we are using the storage that *pA and Storage occupy to construct *pNotC1.

Is *pNotC1 nested-within *pA or Storage?

*pNotC1 is not a subobject of *pA; the subobject was pA->c1. *pA does not provide storage for *pNotC1 as only arrays can do that. So the lifetime of *pA ends.

We are accessing *pNotC1 within Storage, *pNotC1 is being provided storage by Storage, and hence is nested-within Storage. So Storage continues to live.

Q: BigQuery issue: shwoing : Incompatible table partitioning specification A:

From your error logs, your target table is day partitioned on field forecast_start and clustered on customer_id - Expects partitioning specification interval(type:day,field:forecast_start) clustering(customer_id) -

BQ API - Use these reference to update your job config to use both clustering and paritioning

https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/samples/bigquery-load-table-partitioned

https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/querying-clustered-tables#python

Q: Does spring sometimes do some slow processes before and after controller method execution? A:

Garbage Collector + Java heap

First off, Spring is running inside a Java JVM so you have to deal with the garbage collector which depending on conditions gets called when it wants/needs to get called... And this further depends on the ram + mxm (assigned memory) of the specific machine/container you are running on. (I know I am oversimplifying this here...)

k8s environment with 50 parallel requests

Let's look the the following quote from your question:

This behaviour was only captured while the application is running in k8s environment, on my local machine under the same load (which is currently just 50 parallel requests) this never happens.

Pod in which our application is running uses maximum of 1 CPU and 2GB of memory.

You are running inside a k8 container. This makes matters worse... java-virtualization (memory management/GC) + (worker-thread orchestration) on top of...K8 container orchestration/shared-resources...

Additionally, a comment mentioned by @Pankaj caught my eye:

CFS CPU throttling, not Spring. With 1 CPU limit, K8s freezes all threads once the quota is used up each 100ms period. 50 concurrent requests will exhaust that fast.

Kubernetes CPU throttling

Following the comment from @Pankaj, I am going to cite an article on CPU throttling (especially as you only have 1 cpu but are doing stress testing).

Below, are the key takeaways from the article Kubernetes CPU Throttling: What it is, and Best Practices ( Learn to manage CPU resources in Kubernetes to ensure smooth workloads, optimize performance, make strategic CPU choices, and monitor CPU throttlin )

  • CPU throttling in Kubernetes happens when a container tries to use more CPU than its configured CPU limit.
  • Causes the system to slow the container instead of letting it consume more resources.
  • Can significantly degrade application performance because workloads are forced to run slower.
  • The main way to prevent throttling is by carefully configuring CPU requests.
  • Kubernetes doesn’t natively report throttling events. You need monitoring tools and CPU utilization metrics to detect when throttling is happening.*"

From Kubernetes CPU Throttling: What it is, and Best Practices

What can you do?

Monitoring

Again, the specific article I cite above, goes into depth on this.

First off, you need to use **monitoring tools **in order to have better information about what is happening. Tools like graphana hooked up to your infrastructure + microservices/application. I'll assume you do the appropriate configurations, and after - you should have a graphana where you can analyze metrics as they describe here .

Additionally, you can use other tools such as:(https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_top/) .

kubectl top . Display resource (CPU/memory) usage.

This command provides a view of recent resource consumption for nodes and pods. It fetches metrics from the Metrics Server, which aggregates this data from the kubelet on each node. The Metrics Server must be installed and running in the cluster for this command to work.

Resources assigned vs Load

Try to add more nodes and/or VCPUs. Or decrease the number of requests (and see the behavior).

Autoscaling

Configure autoscaling so that your cluster can increase if it is needed. (This is basically the same as adding more nodes/vcpus but it happens automatically based on rules. And it can also scale downwards when demands goes down).

thread-pool vs context switching

I noticed also in your question the following:

(which is currently just 50 parallel requests) this never happens

If you had multiple CPUs, I would suggest increasing your thread pool size. However, since you only have 1 CPU, this means you probably have 50 different requests fighting over CPU resources... (well, actually all the available worker threads trying to service the various requests).

Not Spring MVC Asynch

I also noticed another thing in your question. Specifically, the JDBC query in the main business logic (annotated below):

**But, unless you explicitly have code that utilizes @Asynch (or something similar).. I think we can rule this out and focus more on CPU throttling **

Summery

The first thing I would do is assign more resources... the more the better. And re-run your experiment. If you can't assign more resources, decrease the amount of concurrent requests... see the behavior with 1 request. 10 requests. 25 requests...etc..

And finally, monitor and collect valuable metrics.

Disclaimer

I am heavily citing/referencing from the article: Kubernetes CPU Throttling: What it is, and Best Practices ( Learn to manage CPU resources in Kubernetes to ensure smooth workloads, optimize performance, make strategic CPU choices, and monitor CPU throttlin )
